# Autoencoder Summary
An autoencoder is a generative model comprising two key components: an encoder ($E_{\phi}:{\mathcal {X}}\rightarrow {\mathcal {Z}}$) and a decoder ($D_{\theta}:{\mathcal {Z}}\rightarrow {\mathcal {X}}$). The encoder maps an input message ($\mathbf{x}$) from the input space ($\mathcal{X}$) to a latent code ($\mathbf{z}$) in the latent space ($\mathcal{Z}$), while the decoder attempts to reconstruct the message ($\mathbf{x}' = D_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})$). Training involves minimizing a loss function, $L(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E} *{x\sim \mu* {\text{ref}}}[d(x, D_{\theta}(E_{\phi}(x)))]$, where $\mu_{\text{ref}}$ is a reference probability distribution and $d$ is a reconstruction quality function.
The architecture is typically undercomplete ($\text{dimension}(\mathcal{Z}) < \text{dimension}(\mathcal{X})$) to enforce dimensionality reduction, allowing the autoencoder to potentially generate messages indistinguishable from real data by feeding its decoder arbitrary latent codes ($\mathbf{z}$). Variations exist to improve performance, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), which treat the latent space as a mixture of distributions, and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), which enforce that the latent codes are sparse. Other notable variants include Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) and Contractive Autoencoders (CAEs), which employ different reconstruction criteria to improve feature representation.
